title: Similar Areas and Volumes

findings.finding: The opening does not rehearse finding a missing quantity in an equivalent ratio, although the worked example uses this directly to complete its ratio table.
findings.breakdown: The example moves from 1:9 to 10:90. Students must know to multiply both entries by 10; the investigation checks forming and simplifying ratios but does not check this missing-entry operation.
findings.checked: Checked all supplied teaching. The p3 investigation rehearses calculating areas and forming and simplifying ratios. No opening item asks students to complete an equivalent ratio, and no preceding topic supplies a recent review or exercise.
findings.assumptions: Equivalent-ratio scaling is prior knowledge from the course's ratio work. This substantial prerequisite merits a short recall check under the stated teacher-led delivery. Calculator access does not affect the finding.

repair.proposal: Before p3-investigation, add: 'Complete the equivalent ratios and show the multiplier applied to both terms: a) 1:4 = 3:___; b) 2:5 = 10:___; c) 3:2 = ___:10.' Expected entries: 12, 25, 15. These three short items fit within a one-page opening review.

findings.doneWhen: The opening checks that students can apply the same multiplier to both ratio terms to find a missing quantity.

findings.finding: Practice requires recovering length ratios from area and volume ratios, but the teaching models only the forward square and cube relationships.
findings.breakdown: At p6-q3c-node, students must recognise that 45/20 is the square of the length factor rather than apply it directly to the given length. The volume table later requires the corresponding cube-root decision. Neither inverse operation is explicitly connected to similarity before it is needed.
findings.checked: Checked the complete supplied teaching and the targeted practice. p4-information and p4-example-triangle model lengths to areas; p9-ratio-definition and p9-volume-example model lengths to volumes. Earlier inverse-area practice asks for the method but supplies no teaching of it. A general forward relationship does not model choosing the appropriate root.
findings.assumptions: Square roots and cube roots are prior arithmetic knowledge; selecting them to reverse similarity scaling is the unsupported variant. Calculator access does not supply that decision.

repair.proposal: Before p6-q3c-node, add: 'Two similar figures have areas 8 cm² and 18 cm². A corresponding side of the smaller figure is 6 cm. Area ratio = 8:18 = 4:9. Area ratios square length ratios, so length ratio = √4:√9 = 2:3. The larger side is 6 × 3/2 = 9 cm.' Before p12-q12-root, add the volume counterpart: 'Volume ratios cube length ratios. To recover lengths, take cube roots: volume ratio 8:125 gives length ratio ∛8:∛125 = 2:5, and therefore area ratio 4:25.'

findings.doneWhen: Before each first inverse task, students see why the appropriate root recovers the length ratio and how that ratio is subsequently used.

findings.finding: Extend the integer-dimension task by asking students to find every solution and justify completeness.
findings.breakdown: Changing 'some values' to all possible values adds an explanation of the constraints rather than another routine calculation.
findings.checked: The area ratio is 150/24 = 25/4, giving positive length factor 5/2. Integer larger dimensions require both smaller dimensions to be even. The even ordered factor pairs of 24 are exactly (2,12), (4,6), (6,4), and (12,2). The task uses the inverse-area relationship already required by the topic.
findings.assumptions: Dimensions are positive integers, with a corresponding to c and b corresponding to d.

repair.proposal: After p7-q7, offer: 'Two similar rectangles have areas 24 cm² and 150 cm². Their corresponding dimensions are a,b and c,d, all positive integers. Find every ordered quadruple (a,b,c,d), and explain why there are no others.' Expected answer: (2,12,5,30), (4,6,10,15), (6,4,15,10), and (12,2,30,5). Since c=5a/2 and d=5b/2, both a and b must be even; listing their factor pairs with ab=24 proves completeness.

findings.doneWhen: The optional task asks for all solutions and includes a valid completeness argument.

findings.finding: Generalise how uniform scaling changes surface area per unit volume.
findings.breakdown: This explains the square-versus-cube relationship underlying the preceding cooling question.
findings.checked: For positive linear scale factor k, surface area becomes k²A and volume becomes k³V. Their quotient is A/(kV), giving one-half, one-tenth, and twice the original quotient for k=2, 10, and 1/2 respectively. Only the taught scaling laws and ordinary algebra are needed.
findings.assumptions: A and V are the positive surface area and volume of a solid, and k>0.

repair.proposal: After p13-q14-c, offer: 'A solid has surface area A and volume V. A similar solid is made with positive linear scale factor k. Express its surface area per unit volume in terms of A, V and k. What happens when k=2, k=10 and k=1/2? Explain why.' Expected answer: k²A/(k³V)=A/(kV). The quotient becomes one-half, one-tenth, and twice its original value because volume gains one additional factor of k.

findings.doneWhen: The optional task connects the numerical cooling example to the general inverse dependence on linear scale factor.
